title: Choosing where to build a shelter or make camp
asks: where should i build my shelter
how to pick a campsite in a survival situation
best place to put a shelter
is it safe to camp in a dry creek bed
should i camp in the valley bottom or up higher
picking a bivy spot in snow
were do i set up shelter for the nite
need to hole up for the night, where is a safe spot, over
answer: Start looking for a shelter site as soon as shelter becomes a priority, and make camp early so you have plenty of time to build.
A good site has enough materials for the type of shelter you need, and is large enough and level enough to lie down and protect your equipment.
Choose a site that gives protection from sun, wind, rain and snow.
Choose a site free of dead trees that may fall. Look for loose rocks, dead limbs or other material that could fall on the shelter.
Choose an area free from the threat of avalanches, rockslides, mudslides and flash floods, and clear of high-water marks.
Avoid low-lying areas that may be a cold sump. Cold air settles on low ground, as in the bottom of deep valleys.
Choose a site free from insects, reptiles and poisonous plants. Thick, brushy, low ground harbors more insects. Inspect the site for venomous snakes, ticks, mites, scorpions and stinging ants.
To limit insects, the Army field sanitation manual says to occupy areas away from insect breeding areas such as natural bodies of water, and to avoid areas with high grass or dense vegetation.
Prefer a site that is suitable for signaling and recovery and has adequate food and water.
Use natural shelter such as caves or rock ledges if available. Overhanging ledges, fallen logs and tree wells can also shield you from the elements immediately.
In open country, set up in the lee of a natural windbreak, such as a depression or the downwind side of a ridge or hill. Where there is no natural windbreak, build one with snow or blocks of snow.

In snow-covered mountains, or when snowfall is imminent, always examine a slope's potential for an avalanche before camping on it. Lee slopes may offer shelter in high winds, but wind-driven snow deposited on them can increase the avalanche hazard.

In cold regions, spruce and pine forest is preferable: these trees generally grow on well-drained soil and keep their needles year-round, giving better protection from wind and bad weather than deciduous trees that lose their leaves in winter.
Prepare the site: brush away rocks and twigs from the sleeping area and cut back overhanging vegetation.
If the fire will be outside the shelter, place the shelter opening 90 degrees to the prevailing wind. This reduces the chance of sparks and smoke blowing into the shelter if the wind reverses.
With any lean-to type shelter, place its back side into the wind.
warnings: Avalanche terrain: FEMA says to avoid areas of increased risk, like slopes steeper than 30 degrees or areas downhill of steep slopes, and to watch for signs of increased danger, including recent avalanches and shooting cracks along slopes.
During landslide conditions, avoid rock ledges, the bases of steep slopes, ravines, drainages and narrow canyons.
If you expect flooding, seek high ground right away.
It is unwise to build a fire in or near aircraft or vehicle wreckage, especially if it is used as a shelter: spilled lubricants or fuels may ignite.

quotes.text: When isolated persons have prioritized shelter as a necessity, they must start looking for it as soon as possible. A good shelter site will contain enough materials to improvise the type of shelter needed as well as be large enough and level enough for the isolated person to lie down and protect their equipment. When selecting a shelter site, consider whether the site
Making camp early so that you have plenty of time to build a shelter.
Provides elemental sun, wind, rain, and snow protection.
Is free of dead trees that may fall.
Is located in an area free from threat of avalanches, rockslides, mudslides, Flash-flood areas and high-water marks.
Is free from insects, reptiles, and poisonous plants. Low-lying areas that may be a cold sump.
Is suitable for signaling and recovery.
Contains adequate food and water.

Site preparation includes brushing away rocks and twigs from the sleeping area and cutting back overhanging vegetation. Look for loose rocks, dead limbs, coconuts, or other material that could fall on the shelter. Remember thick, brushy, low ground also harbors more insects. Inspect the site for venomous snakes, ticks, mites, scorpions, and stinging ants.
Areas lying in the bottom of deep valleys and large lakes should be avoided due to masses of cold air settling on low ground (also known as a temperature inversion).
Use natural shelters such as caves or rock ledges if available. If they are not, build a temporary improvised shelter.
Natural formations can also shield the isolated person from the elements immediately, to include overhanging ledges, fallen logs, caves, and tree wells.

If establishing a patrol base in open areas, tents should be pitched (or shelters constructed) in the lee of natural windbreaks such as depressions or the downwind side of eskers, ridges, and hills. Where no natural windbreaks exist, dig tents into the snow as deeply as possible or construct windbreaks with snow or blocks of snow.

During high winds, lee slopes may offer shelter. However, they can also increase exposure to avalanche hazards if wind-driven snow is deposited on lee slopes. If the slope is steep enough, the snow eventually slides. In snowcovered mountains or when snowfall is imminent, always examine a slope’s potential for an avalanche prior to establishing a bivouac upon it.

Spruce and pine forests are preferable for a variety of reasons; one being that these types of trees generally grow on well-drained soil. Another reason is they retain their needles year-round, offering better concealment and protection from wind and inclement weather than deciduous trees that lose their leaves during the winter months.

If a fire is placed outside the shelter, the opening of the shelter should be placed 90 degrees to the prevailing wind. This reduces the chances of sparks and smoke being blown into the shelter if the wind reverses direction in the morning and evening, which frequently occurs in mountainous areas.
As with all lean-to type shelters, be sure to place the lean-to’s backside into the wind.
It is unwise to build a fire in or near an aircraft or vehicle wreckage, especially if it is used as a shelter. The possibility of igniting spilled lubricants or fuels is great.
During landslide conditions, avoid rock ledges, bases of steep slopes, ravines, drainages, or narrow canyons.
Watch for signs of increased danger, including recent avalanches and shooting cracks along slopes. Avoid areas of increased risk like slopes steeper than 30 degrees or areas downhill of steep slopes.
Never drive around barricades. Local responders use them to safely direct traffic out of flooded areas. Seek high ground right away if you expect flooding.
Occupying areas away from insect/arthropod breeding areas such as natural bodies of water. Avoiding areas with high grass or dense vegetation.

conflict: Natural shelter under rock: the Army manuals say to use natural shelters such as caves, rock ledges and overhanging ledges (TC 21-3 2025, ATP 3-50.21 2018). FEMA P-2064 (2020, landslide section) says 'During landslide conditions, avoid rock ledges, bases of steep slopes, ravines, drainages, or narrow canyons.' The card gives both: the Army line in the answer, the FEMA line as a warning. Water nearby: ATP 3-50.21 lists a site that 'Contains adequate food and water'; ATP 4-25.12 says to occupy areas 'away from insect/arthropod breeding areas such as natural bodies of water'. The card gives both.

review.notes: Pass. Each line checked against ATP 3-50.21 ch. 6, TC 21-3 ch. 5/7, ATP 4-25.12 and FEMA P-2064; meaning kept. Both real conflicts are shown attributed in the card: Army 'use caves and rock ledges' vs FEMA landslide 'avoid rock ledges'; ATP 3-50.21 'adequate food and water' vs ATP 4-25.12 'away from natural bodies of water' for insects. Avalanche lines match the snow-cave card (TC 21-3 5-12 lee slopes; FEMA 30 degrees). Notes for the drafter: (1) record in the conflict field one more passage, ATP 3-50.21 7-6 (desert evasion): 'Hide or seek shelter in dry washes (wadis)...' - evasion context that contradicts the flash-flood rule; correctly not used, but it should be listed. (2) The 'dry creek bed' ask is answered only implicitly (flash-flood areas, high-water marks); no kit text says it more directly, so this is acceptable. (3) The kit has no lightning site guidance outside FEMA's buildings/vehicles advice, so nothing is missing on that point. Kind fact correct.
